displayQuote: The problem with socialism is that you eventually run out of other people's money

meta.title: Who really said "The problem with socialism is that you eventually run out of other people's money"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Thatcher’s idea, and she said it twice on the record — but never in this sentence. The famous version is a paraphrase of a 1976 TV interview.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The problem with socialism is that you eventually run out of other people's money'?
meta.ogDescription: What she actually said: “Socialist governments traditionally do make a financial mess. They always run out of other people’s money.” February 1976.

answer.label: Margaret Thatcher — but this is a paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The idea is hers and she put it on the record twice, but neither time in this sentence. Wikiquote’s sourced Thatcher material transcribes her 1976 television interview as “Socialist governments traditionally do make a financial mess. They always run out of other people’s money. It’s quite a characteristic of them,” and adds a note in its own voice: that last sentence “is widely paraphrased as ‘The trouble/problem with socialism is that eventually you run out of other people’s money.’” The line you know is the paraphrase, not the quotation.

source.heading: What she actually said — twice

docMeta.dd: “Socialist governments traditionally do make a financial mess. They always run out of other people’s money. It’s quite a characteristic of them.”
TV interview for Thames Television, This Week · 5 February 1976
Speech to the Conservative Party Conference, 10 October 1975: “They’ve got the usual Socialist disease — they’ve run out of other people’s money.”
A paraphrase. Wikiquote flags it as such in a note attached to the 1976 entry.

Both Wikiquote entries cite the Margaret Thatcher Foundation’s transcripts. That archive is blocked by this run’s network policy, so the wordings above are Wikiquote’s transcriptions and the dates are Wikiquote’s — neither was checked against the original transcript here.
source.excerptNote: Note what the paraphrase does. Thatcher was making an empirical claim about how socialist governments have behaved — “traditionally,” “quite a characteristic of them.” The rewrite turns that into a claim about socialism as a system, with an inevitability (“eventually”) she did not put there. It is a sharper sentence and a stronger claim, and she did not make it.

author.name: Margaret Thatcher
author.heading: About Margaret Thatcher
author.bio: Margaret Thatcher became leader of the Conservative Party in 1975 and Prime Minister in 1979. Both documented versions of this line come from the years in between, when she was Leader of the Opposition and sharpening the arguments that would define her premiership. She was a genuinely quotable speaker — which is why it is worth noticing how often the sentence attributed to her is tidier than the sentence she said. The rewrite is usually shorter, more symmetrical, and claims more.

misattribution.heading: How the paraphrase replaced the quotation
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here — the speaker is right and the idea is right. What changed is the sentence, and the change made it claim more than she did.

items.why: Wikiquote attaches an explicit note to the sourced entry: the line “is widely paraphrased” in this form. The rewrite swaps her claim about governments for a claim about socialism itself, and adds the word “eventually.”

misattribution.truthLine: If you want Thatcher on this, you can have her verbatim — the 1976 wording ↗ is documented and quotable. The popular sentence is somebody else’s edit of it.

context.heading: Why the edit matters
lead: When Thatcher gave this interview in February 1976 she had led the Conservative Party since 1975, and Britain was in the middle of the sterling crisis ↗ that would end with Callaghan’s Labour government borrowing $3.9 billion from the International Monetary Fund. Her charge that socialist governments “always run out of other people’s money” was an argument about a specific record in a specific country, delivered on a current-affairs programme to an audience living through it.

The paraphrase strips the timing out and makes it timeless. “Socialist governments traditionally” becomes “socialism”; a pattern she claimed to observe becomes an outcome that arrives “eventually,” by necessity. That is a bigger claim, and a more useful one for whoever is quoting it — which is generally how paraphrases drift.
detailsBody: It is worth knowing that Thatcher used the phrase at least twice, four months apart, and that the earlier outing is the punchier one: “They’ve got the usual Socialist disease — they’ve run out of other people’s money,” to the Conservative Party Conference on 10 October 1975. Wikiquote attaches its paraphrase note to that entry.
Because she said it more than once, in more than one form, there is no single “original” to restore. What can be said cleanly is that the sentence in circulation matches neither documented version.

Both Wikiquote entries cite transcripts held by the Margaret Thatcher Foundation. That site is blocked by this run’s network policy, so the dates and wordings on this page are Wikiquote’s transcription rather than a reading of the source transcripts.
context.pull: She said socialist governments always run out of other people’s money. The rewrite says socialism does — eventually, inevitably. That is not the same sentence.

Wikiquote transcribes her 10 October 1975 Conservative Party Conference speech as containing "They've got the usual Socialist disease - they've run out of other people's money", and attaches the note: "The last sentence is widely paraphrased as 'The trouble/problem with socialism is that eventually you run out of other people's money.'"

Margaret Thatcher was Leader of the Conservative Party from 1975 to 1990 and Prime Minister from 4 May 1979 to 28 November 1990; born 13 October 1925, died 8 April 2013.
Wikipedia's 1976 sterling crisis article states that Callaghan's Labour government had to borrow $3.9 billion from the International Monetary Fund while implementing significant spending cuts.

Thatcherism is the British conservative ideology named after Margaret Thatcher, associated with monetarism and described as part of the neoliberal movement, covering her government from 1979 to her resignation in 1990.
